trigger_mechanism_explained.question: How was the successful city-site-profiles PATCH actually triggered, given computer left_click is unreliable in this environment?
trigger_mechanism_explained.answer: Neither `computer left_click` (CDP coordinate-based, confirmed unreliable in this session) nor `document.dispatchEvent(...)` was used for this save. The actual mechanism, used consistently for every successful button interaction in this session (save buttons, edit links, remove-cover buttons, modal close icons, filter toggles), was: `javascript_tool` executing page-context JS that does `Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('button')).find(b => b.textContent.trim() === '保存').click()` -- i.e. calling the native `HTMLElement.prototype.click()` method directly ON the target DOM node (not on `document`, not via CDP synthetic coordinates). `.click()` called this way dispatches a real (bubbling, but isTrusted:false) click event AT that element, which bubbles up and is picked up by React's delegated synthetic event listener the same way a real user click would be -- React does not check `event.isTrusted` when constructing SyntheticEvent. This is why button-triggered saves worked reliably throughout the session while coordinate-based clicks and document-level keyboard dispatch did not.
trigger_mechanism_explained.field_edit_mechanism: Text field edits (e.g. introHeading) used the native property setter trick: `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(window.HTMLInputElement.prototype, 'value').set.call(el, newValue)` followed by `el.dispatchEvent(new Event('input', {bubbles:true}))` and `dispatchEvent(new Event('change', {bubbles:true}))` -- this is the standard technique to make a React-controlled input register a change (a plain `el.value = x` assignment does NOT notify React because React overrides the native value setter to track its own state).

subclaim_B_escape_key_only_closes_picker.why_not_verified: No live, keyboard-triggered confirmation was obtained in this session. Two attempts were made; on audit review, the two do NOT carry equal evidentiary weight -- see corrected methodology below.

attempt_1_document_dispatchEvent.corrected_analysis: This attempt was methodologically broken from the start and its failure carries ZERO diagnostic information, independent of any environment issue. Dispatching an event with `document` as the target means `document` IS the event's target: the event only travels through document's own capture/target phase and then bubbles toward `window` -- it can NEVER reach listeners on DESCENDANT nodes (such as the Modal's or Drawer's own wrapper divs, which are children of document.body, i.e. descendants of document). The original report incorrectly treated this as informative evidence of an environment limitation; it is not -- it was guaranteed to fail regardless of environment, because it was dispatched at the wrong node in the DOM tree. This correction was pointed out by the independent audit and is accepted.

attempt_2_computer_key_action.what_was_done: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer{action:'key', text:'Escape'} -- a CDP-level (Chrome DevTools Protocol) key event, which is normally routed to whichever DOM node currently has focus (confirmed via document.activeElement to be the modal's own search input at the time), not dependent on manually picking a dispatch target the way attempt 1 was.
attempt_2_computer_key_action.corrected_analysis: This is the only one of the two attempts that is actually informative. Because CDP key events target the focused element via the browser's real input pipeline (not a JS-level dispatchEvent target choice), a failure here is more plausibly attributable to the same environment limitation already established by the screenshot-compositing failure (i.e. a tab that is not the 'displayed/composited' surface may not reliably receive synthetic OS-level input at all, regardless of DOM focus state) -- but this is still a plausible explanation for an inconclusive result, NOT proof that the underlying Arco/React code is correct. It only means: no positive confirmation was obtained, and the most likely reason is environmental, not that the code is provably right.
attempt_2_computer_key_action.evidentiary_weight: LOW / suggestive only -- does not amount to REAL_EVIDENCE for subclaim B.

code_level_reasoning_supporting_but_not_.arco Drawer source (node_modules/@arco-d: Drawer has its OWN independent onKeyDown handler bound directly to its own portal wrapper div (also escToExit-gated), not to document and not to any ancestor shared with Modal's wrapper
code_level_reasoning_supporting_but_not_.reasoning: Modal and Drawer are separate DOM portal subtrees (both default to document.body as popup container) each with an independently-scoped onKeyDown handler. A keydown originating inside the Modal's subtree can only bubble through the Modal's own DOM ancestors, not into the Drawer's separate subtree -- architecturally Escape cannot double-close both. Combined with the explicit stopPropagation() call, this is a sound architectural argument.
code_level_reasoning_supporting_but_not_.status: This remains CODE-LEVEL REASONING, explicitly NOT equivalent to REAL_EVIDENCE. Per the audit's instruction, subclaim B is labeled NOT_VERIFIED and must not be folded into an overall 'passed' summary for Step 8.
